tip: For 'behind himself' Dutch uses 'zich', not 'hem': 'achter zich'.
'Proberen' connects to a following verb with 'te': 'proberen ... te komen'.
Here 'voor' marks a deadline, meaning 'by Friday', not 'in front of': 'voor vrijdag'.
'Niet' normally follows the time word: it is 'vandaag niet', not 'niet vandaag'.
'Wel' is the positive counter to 'niet', affirming what was just denied.
'Pas' means 'not until' or 'only then': 'pas ... als je achttien bent'.
'Uittrekken' is separable: the prefix 'uit' moves to the end: 'trekt ... uit'.
With no article, Dutch negates a noun with 'geen', not 'niet': 'geen wifi' = no wifi.
'Vanwege' means 'because of' and takes a noun ('het slechte weer'); 'omdat' would need a full clause.
Dutch asks the time with 'hoe laat', literally 'how late': 'hoe laat het is'.
'Vijf voor twaalf' also means 'it is almost too late' figuratively.
'Sinds' = since, marking the start point of an ongoing situation: 'sinds mijn vijfde'.
An adjective can stand alone as a noun: 'de langzame' = the slow one, with 'trein' left out.
Fixed phrase 'zich zorgen maken over' = to worry about: 'maakt zich zorgen over'.
'Per se' (from Latin) means absolutely or no matter what: 'hij wil per se'.
'Hoeven' means 'have to' only in the negative, and pairs with 'te': 'hoeft niet ... te komen'.
Dutch says 'ongelijk hebben' for 'to be wrong', literally 'have wrong': 'ik ongelijk had'.
'Zich vervelen' = to be bored – Dutch needs the 'zich', English does not.
'Zich schamen voor' = to be ashamed of; the 'zich' is required: 'schaamt zich voor'.
'Wat dies meer zij' = be that as it may – literary.
'Zich afvragen' = to wonder – literally 'ask oneself': 'vraagt zich af'.
'Lang niet gezien' is a fixed greeting for long time no see. It drops the 'hebben' that 'gezien' would normally need.
'Naartoe' adds the sense of to or toward: 'nergens naartoe' = nowhere to go, 'ergens naartoe' = somewhere to go.
After 'waarom' the verb moves to the end: 'waarom hij boos is', not 'waarom hij is boos'.
'Voorbereiden' splits: the prefix 'voor' moves to the end, so the command is 'bereid je voor', not 'voorbereid je'.
'Wel' is the positive counter to a negative. Here 'geen vlees maar wel vis' means no meat but yes to fish.
Starting a sentence with something other than the subject flips the order, so the verb comes first: 'zou ik', not 'ik zou'.
'Met' for means of transport: 'met de auto', 'met de trein'.
'Geen' and 'meer' wrap around the noun to mean none left: 'geen melk meer' means no more milk.
'Mogen' means to be allowed; with 'niet' it means not allowed: 'mogen ... niet fietsen' = you may not cycle.
